styles.name: 1970s Japanese Super-Robot TV Anime
styles.visual_description: Huge chrome-faced robots, candy-colored enemy fortresses, painted explosions, thick cel outlines, heroic freeze-frames, recycled launch sequences. Every cockpit glows like a toy commercial. Melancholy backgrounds: empty industrial lots, sunset harbors, schoolyards under attack.
styles.wrongness: The contradiction between apocalyptic war drama and the obvious need to sell die-cast robot toys.
styles.historical_context: Weekly TV anime needed repeatable footage, sponsor-friendly silhouettes, and instantly legible transformations. Faded as mecha design became more militarized and prestige-driven.
styles.prompt_seed: 1977 Japanese weekly super-robot TV anime, giant chrome red-and-blue robot launching from an underground school hangar at sunset, thick cel paint, bold toyetic silhouettes, reused transformation footage, painted smoke bursts, limited animation, dramatic zooms, analog broadcast softness, heroic but slightly lonely tone.
accurate_artifacts: cel animation dust and scratches (physical cells handled manually)
limited animation stillness (3-6 cels per second held frames)
cel edge shadow visible on multiplane composites
film grain from 16mm reversal or negative stock
sprocket jitter on fast camera pans
broadcast tape generation loss (dubbed from film to air)
forbidden_artifacts: motion blur (limited animation = held cels, not motion)
styles.color_science: 16mm Eastmancolor negative stock — warm saturated primaries, slight magenta shift in shadows, cel paint colors (bright chrome yellow, candy red, electric blue) punch through the film stock's warm bias

styles.name: 1980s Direct-to-Video Cyberpunk OVA
styles.visual_description: Neon rain, motorcycle gangs, biomechanical alleyways, oily shadows, over-detailed city backgrounds, reflective helmets, cable nests. Characters barely move while camera pans across impossible amounts of hand-painted machinery.
styles.wrongness: The world looks more expensive than the animation budget can support.
styles.historical_context: Economic miracle of the rental-video era: niche adult-skewing anime could be too violent, too stylish, or too strange for TV. Faded when OVA market collapsed and digital pipelines made grime too clean.
styles.prompt_seed: 1988 Japanese direct-to-video cyberpunk OVA, lone courier in a black raincoat walking through a neon alley full of cables and vending machines, magenta-green palette, wet asphalt reflections, slow pan over hyper-detailed painted background, held cels, VHS chroma bleed, heavy shadow, doomed electric mood.
accurate_artifacts: cel dust and scratches (hand-painted cels on glass backgrounds)
airbrush gradient banding on painted backgrounds
limited animation with sudden fluid motion bursts (expensive key frames saved for action)
VHS generation loss (OVA distribution was VHS rental)
tracking noise bars on VHS playback
color-under chroma bleed from VHS color encoding
forbidden_artifacts: lens flare (cel animation, not live-action lens)
motion blur (held cels with sudden motion, not continuous blur)
styles.color_science: 35mm negative stock — rich blacks, deep cyans and magentas, neon highlights bloom against dark backgrounds. OVA budgets allowed theatrical-grade film with saturated cel paints (neon pink, electric cyan, chrome silver)

styles.name: 1980s Bubble-Economy City-Pop Anime
styles.visual_description: Glass elevators, pastel condos, imported sports cars, rooftop pools, department-store atriums, soft airbrush lighting. Young adults staring wistfully at skyline sunsets like consumer abundance has somehow made them lonelier.
styles.wrongness: Aspirational wealth treated as emotional emptiness.
styles.historical_context: Japan's bubble economy, music-video cross-promotion, lifestyle magazines, high-end urban fantasy. Faded after bubble burst when optimism became historically haunted.

airbrush glow on painted backgrounds (soft gradients)
broadcast tape transfer artifacts (Betacam SP dub)
slight color shift from telecine transfer
forbidden_artifacts: VHS tracking noise (broadcast-grade Betacam SP, not consumer VHS)
styles.color_science: 16mm Eastmancolor + Betacam SP broadcast transfer — pastel pinks, peach skies, lavender dusk, chrome highlights. Airbrushed soft gradients with warm sunset palette. Film stock warmth amplifies the aspirational golden-hour mood

styles.name: 1990s Anime CD-ROM / Visual Novel Cutscene
styles.visual_description: Static rooms, cursor-like pacing, soft dithering, jewel-toned gradients, stiff character portraits, blinking animation, low-resolution UI frames. Melodramatic still images that feel trapped inside obsolete software.
styles.wrongness: Intimacy delivered through interface friction.
styles.historical_context: PC-98 games, CD-ROM extras, visual novels, multimedia discs where storage limits shaped drama. Faded as full-motion video, higher-resolution art, and console-standard pipelines absorbed its weird stillness.

static text box overlay with aliased font rendering
looping ambient audio track (short sample loop)
styles.color_science: 256-color VGA/SVGA palette — dithered gradients, limited color depth, blue-black backgrounds with cyan UI highlights. Character portraits use anime color palette compressed into 8-bit. Slight color banding in skin tones and sky gradients

styles.visual_description: Third-generation tape softness, blown-out whites, fuzzy subtitles, tracking noise, color drift, hardcoded translator notes. Action scenes half-swallowed by analog blur. Image feels passed hand to hand, not distributed.

styles.historical_context: Informal fan networks, bootleg circulation, anime clubs, convention rooms, mail-order tape culture. Faded when DVDs, torrents, and streaming made access cleaner and less communal.

text overlay burn-in from subtitling hardware

styles.name: 1990s Late-Night Psychological Anime

styles.wrongness: Budget-saving stillness becomes existential terror.
styles.historical_context: Late-night slots allowed stranger, moodier, less toy-driven anime with smaller audiences and more experimental pacing. Faded as techniques became absorbed into prestige anime and internet-era 'dark anime' shorthand.

styles.name: 1970s Shōjo Melodrama Anime

rose petal overlay (physical cutouts animated frame-by-frame)

styles.wrongness: The visible pain of an industry switching tools mid-sentence.
styles.historical_context: Studios moved from cel to digital production under brutal TV deadlines. Faded as digital pipelines matured and the awkward transitional look became something everyone tried to forget.

plastic skin highlights (digital shading, not painted)
stiff mouth-flap animation (digital lip sync, limited frames)

awkward early-CG elements (3D vehicles/objects inserted into 2D)

styles.name: 1980s Idol Anime Music Video

styles.historical_context: Idol culture, record-label promotion, TV specials, anime's ability to turn pop personas into endlessly reusable characters. Faded as idol media, anime music videos, and character franchises became more polished and vertically integrated.

styles.color_science: 16mm Eastmancolor + Betacam SP — bright saturated primaries (hot pink, electric blue, chrome yellow). Idol anime pushed color saturation for energetic music video feel. Broadcast transfer maintains vibrancy

styles.name: 1990s Low-Poly Anime-Adjacent JRPG Cutscene
styles.visual_description: Blocky 3D temples, pre-rendered skies, anime portrait inserts, low-resolution textures, stiff character turns, dramatic camera swoops. Polygonal monsters moving with strange puppet weight.
styles.wrongness: Epic emotion trapped inside primitive geometry.
styles.historical_context: PlayStation-era JRPGs, CD storage, experimental 3D pipelines, desire to make games feel cinematic before hardware could fully support it. Faded as real-time graphics improved and low-poly became either nostalgia or stylization rather than necessity.

styles.name: 1980s American Corporate Training VHS Melodrama
styles.visual_description: Beige conference rooms, tube-TV glare, soft fluorescent lighting, bad lapel mics, over-bright ties, fake office plants, ring binders. Actors speak like every sentence was approved by HR legal. Locked-off camera, slow edits, every conflict solved by a laminated procedure.
styles.wrongness: Emotional over-seriousness applied to tiny workplace problems: photocopier etiquette treated like a moral crisis.
styles.historical_context: Corporations needed cheap, scalable internal media before digital onboarding. Faded when PowerPoint, LMS platforms, and frictionless web video killed the strange theatricality of the training tape.
styles.prompt_seed: 1987 American corporate training VHS, two office workers in a beige conference room learning an ominous new company policy, fluorescent lighting, soft analog video blur, locked-off tripod camera, awkward pauses, washed-out colors, lapel mic hiss, sincere instructional acting, faint tracking noise, emotionally unsettling but polite.

forbidden_artifacts: lens chromatic aberration (cheap corporate cameras had simple lenses)
shallow depth of field (corporate = everything in focus)

styles.name: 1970s British Public Information Film Doom-Miniature
styles.visual_description: Rainy streets, school uniforms, concrete underpasses, overcast skies, children filmed from too far away, and a narrator who sounds calm while describing catastrophe. Everything feels civic, gray, and fatal.
styles.wrongness: Mismatch between educational intent and folk-horror dread.
styles.historical_context: Public safety campaigns had broadcast access but little budget. Faded as PSAs became friendlier, faster, brand-managed, and less terrifying.

styles.name: 1970s Eastern European Philosophical Sci-Fi Television
styles.visual_description: Sparse sets, silver paper walls, geometric props, heavy dialogue, long silences, strange costumes. Actors stare past each other like they're discussing the fate of consciousness in a municipal theater. Space looks handmade, not spectacular.

styles.name: 1980s Mall Kiosk Demo Video
styles.visual_description: Glossy product close-ups, spinning logos, synth stingers, chrome gradients, fake excitement, and a camera obsessed with hands pressing buttons. The video loops forever because nobody is really watching, yet it tries to sound like the future has arrived.

styles.visual_description: Rubber suits, sparks, smoke pots, miniature city blocks, visible wires, heroic low angles, toy-like vehicles, and painted skies. The monster is physical, heavy, clumsy, and glorious. Buildings crumble like balsa wood, but the emotional stakes are completely sincere.

styles.name: 1990s Hype Williams Hip-Hop Music Video
styles.visual_description: Extreme fish-eye lens, chrome and gold surfaces, shiny suits, helicopter shots over rooftops, strobing neon, oversized jewelry catching every light source. The camera warps space so the artist looks larger than the city behind them. Everything gleams, drips, and reflects.

styles.visual_description: Warm golden tones, slow-motion walks down palm-lined streets, low-rider hydraulics catching sunlight, corner store neon, chain-link fences, basketball courts at dusk.
